vignette:
Richard is a 63-year-old physician, married and practicing internal medicine at a mid-sized urban hospital, who was referred for psychological assessment following what his wife described as a marked and sustained change in his personality over the past two years. The precipitating event occurred when Richard was riding a city bus home from a medical conference - an unusual choice for him, made only because his car was in the shop. The bus was crowded and he had taken a window seat near the middle when, at a downtown stop, a man boarded carrying a backpack and began shouting commands at passengers, ordering them to move to the back, not to use their phones, not to look at him. Richard froze. The man's coat was bulging in a way that Richard, in those suspended seconds, read as a vest. A transit officer eventually subdued the man - it turned out to be a disturbed individual with no weapon - but not before Richard had spent nearly four minutes certain he was about to die in a terrorist attack. He had pressed himself against the window, listening to the shouting, watching the officer's hand move toward his holster, and had experienced what he later described as "the clearest thought I've ever had: that none of us were getting off that bus."

In the weeks that followed, Richard found that the world had reorganized itself around that four-minute certainty. He had come to believe, with a conviction that felt more like knowledge than opinion, that the world is a genuinely dangerous place and that people are not what they seem - that the man on the bus had looked ordinary, had looked like anyone, and that this was precisely the point. These appraisals did not stay abstract. They reached back into the triggers themselves, amplifying them: the sound of raised voices in a hospital corridor, a security guard issuing instructions to a visitor, the distant rumble of a city bus passing the clinic window - each of these now carried the charge of that afternoon, not merely as a reminder but as evidence confirming what Richard had concluded about the world. The loop was self-sealing. Each encounter with a trigger renewed his conviction that danger was everywhere and that people concealed their intentions, and that renewed conviction made the triggers more potent still.

What this meant in practice was a state of sustained physiological and psychological vigilance that had become the texture of his daily life. Inside his own home - a place that had once felt unambiguously safe - Richard now listened for sounds at the perimeter, tracking the creak of the house settling, the approach of a car in the street, any noise that might mean someone was entering. His wife had noticed him checking the locks multiple times before bed. At the hospital, where he spent long hours on a ward that required him to give and receive clear instructions all day, he found himself reacting to the ordinary authority-laden language of medicine - a charge nurse directing him, a colleague asking him to step into a procedure - with a flash of something close to rage, followed by shame. His irritability had begun to affect his relationships with colleagues and, more painfully, with his wife, who told him he had become someone she did not recognize.

The appraisal that his life had been destroyed by what happened on that bus fed back into his hypervigilance, deepening it: if the damage was already total, then the threat that caused it must be real and ongoing, and so he listened harder, trusted less, and found fresh confirmation in each uneasy moment. Richard had stopped riding public transit entirely, and now drove to the hospital even when parking was difficult, rerouting to avoid bus stops. A fleeting awareness that this was narrowing his world sat somewhere at the edge of his thinking, unexamined.

He sought help after his wife told him she was frightened - not of him, but for him. What Richard said he most feared was that the person he had been before the bus was simply gone. What he said he most hoped was that someone could explain why a man who had spent thirty years calmly managing medical emergencies could be undone by four minutes on a city bus.
